abstract_sentences.text: In sampling tasks, it is common for target distributions to be known up to a normalizing constant.
abstract_sentences.transition: Sets the standard setting before the evaluation obstacle.

evidence.anchor: known up to a normalizing constant

abstract_sentences.text: However, in many situations, even evaluating the unnormalized distribution can be costly or infeasible.
abstract_sentences.comparison: Contrasts standard normalizing-constant access with expensive unnormalized evaluation.
abstract_sentences.transition: Narrows the problem from normalization to target evaluation.

abstract_sentences.text: This issue arises in scenarios such as sampling from the Bayesian posterior for tall datasets and the ‘doubly-intractable’ distributions.
abstract_sentences.transition: Supplies the two motivating settings for the method.

evidence.anchor: tall datasets and the doubly-intractable distributions

abstract_sentences.text: In this paper, we begin by observing that seemingly different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms, such as the exchange algorithm, PoissonMH, and TunaMH, can be unified under a simple common procedure.
abstract_sentences.transition: Moves from two settings to the unification insight.

evidence.anchor: unified under a simple common procedure

abstract_sentences.text: We then extend this procedure into a novel framework that allows the use of auxiliary variables in both the proposal and the acceptance–rejection step.
abstract_sentences.comparison: Two computational roles for auxiliary variables.
abstract_sentences.transition: Extends the common procedure into the new framework.

evidence.anchor: both the proposal and the acceptance–rejection step

abstract_sentences.text: Several new MCMC algorithms emerge from this framework that uses estimated gradients to guide the proposal moves.
abstract_sentences.comparison: Gradient-guided proposals versus the earlier common procedure.
abstract_sentences.transition: Instantiates the framework as new algorithms.

evidence.anchor: estimated gradients to guide the proposal moves

abstract_sentences.text: They have demonstrated significantly better performance than existing methods on both synthetic and real datasets.
abstract_sentences.comparison: Existing methods; synthetic and real datasets.
abstract_sentences.transition: Places the empirical performance claim after the method.

abstract_sentences.text: We also develop theory for the new framework and use it to simplify and extend results for existing algorithms.
abstract_sentences.comparison: New framework against results for existing algorithms.

abstract_sentences.text: The code to reproduce the experimental results can be found at https://github.com/ywwes26/Auxiliary-MCMC.
abstract_sentences.transition: Ends with reproducibility access rather than a limitation.

evidence.anchor: code to reproduce the experimental results

abstract_summary.function_sequence: object scope → problem gap → two settings → unification → framework → algorithms → qualitative result → theory → code
abstract_summary.reported_result_type: Qualitative superiority only; no numerical value, uncertainty statement, or test protocol in the abstract.
abstract_summary.strongest_claim_location: Sentence 7, immediately after the two framework/method sentences.

method_moves.description: Section 2 defines target, proposal, current state, auxiliary variable, and estimator ratio.

evidence.anchor: Given target distribution, a proposal q

method_moves.description: Equation (1) supplies the pointwise balance condition and Proposition 1 draws unbiasedness/reversibility.
Connects doubly-intractable and tall-data algorithms while delimiting the identity-involution special case.
Motivates gradient-based proposals because random-walk/independent proposals scale poorly in high dimensions.
Section 3.1 introduces spaces, Ptheta, Ptheta,thetaprime, simulators S1/S2, NULL, and qomega1.
Algorithm 1 samples omega1, proposes theta-prime, samples omega2, and accepts with the joint auxiliary ratio.
Cases 1–3 explain no proposal auxiliary, shared auxiliaries, and independent auxiliaries.
Maps Algorithm 1 to involutive MCMC validity.
Section 3.2.1 constructs locally balanced PoissonMH, then names Poisson–Barker and Poisson–MALA.
Section 3.2.2 constructs Tuna–SGLD from an SGLD proposal plus independent Tuna ratio minibatch.
Identifies skipped acceptance correction with fixed-step SGLD and its systematic bias.
Links the tall-data construction to subsequent numerical experiments and minibatch cost.

formal_objects.target: Generic Π on Θ, instantiated as posterior π(θ|x).
formal_objects.state: θ; auxiliary variables are generated inside a transition rather than stored in the reported chain state.
formal_objects.inputs: θ0, T, simulators S1/S2, Pθ, Pθ,θ-prime, and proposal family qω1.
formal_objects.output: A θ-chain whose transition kernel is claimed reversible with respect to Π.
formal_objects.objective: Avoid direct costly target/gradient evaluation by cancellation within the auxiliary-variable acceptance ratio.

component_problem_map.problem: Low-cost proposal design from an estimated gradient or minibatch.

evidence.anchor: generated to estimate the target ratio

component_problem_map.problem: Preserve detailed balance while expensive target factors cancel.

pseudocode.loop_structure: Algorithms 1–7 have a single MCMC iteration loop; Algorithms 8–9 add a Poisson-ball loop.
pseudocode.complexity: Appendix C states O(B) sampled Poisson variables after one-time alias-table construction.

method_analysis.theory_role: Core causal chain: auxiliary variables create the proposal/ratio factorization; conditional-law closeness controls efficiency loss.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Equation (1)
equation_theory_inventory.statement: Pointwise relation connecting R, π, and reverse auxiliary law.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Algorithm 1 acceptance ratio
equation_theory_inventory.statement: Joint ω1,ω2 ratio used in Algorithm 1.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 1
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Equation (1) holds for every θ and θ-prime.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: R is unbiased for the posterior ratio and K is reversible.
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: Serves as the common-procedure validity statement; no direct empirical theorem test.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 2
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Access to simulators S1/S2 and the specified joint auxiliary construction.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Paux defined by Algorithm 1 is reversible with respect to Π.
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: Algorithms 2 and 3 are declared Cases 2 and 3, respectively.

evidence.anchor: Paux is reversible with respect to Π

equation_theory_inventory.label: Lemma 1
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Same θ, θ-prime pair and the three transition densities.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: paux ≤ pMwG ≤ pideal, implying Peskun ordering.
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: Appendix G.4 later discusses clock-time and iteration-wise rankings.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Theorem 1
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Conditional auxiliary distributions can be compared in TV/KL.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Lower-bounds paux by TV/KL factors times pMwG.
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: Feeds into existing-algorithm spectral-gap propositions, not a direct experimental estimand.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 3
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Exchange algorithm and a uniform set-probability condition.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Gives a TV/spectral-gap lower bound relative to pideal.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 4
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Gives a max of old and KL-derived gap lower bounds.
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: Section 5 evaluates PoissonMH variants but does not estimate the bound.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 5
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Gap(Paux) is lower-bounded by exp{-1/(2χ)} Gap(Pideal).

equation_theory_inventory.label: Theorem 2
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Common stationary distribution Π for PMwG and Paux.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Bounds Gap(Paux) via TV/KL comparison times Gap(PMwG).
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: Theory supplies a cost-versus-iteration interpretation; no direct gap experiment.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 6
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Imported result from Qin et al. (2025).
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Relates Gap(PMwG) to Gibbs and conditional MH gaps.
equation_theory_inventory.proof_location: No new proof in this paper; explicitly attributed to Qin et al. (2025).

evidence.anchor: Corollary 14 and Theorem 15 of Qin et al.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 8
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Bounds Poisson KL by the endpoint pair.

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 9
equation_theory_inventory.assumptions: Product measures Pi and Qi on corresponding measurable spaces.
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: Gives product KL equality and a TV overlap lower bound.

evidence.anchor: Let Pi, Qi be two probability measures

equation_theory_inventory.label: Proposition 10
equation_theory_inventory.conclusion: The modified auxiliary chain remains reversible.
equation_theory_inventory.empirical_correspondence: The main algorithms use min{1,r}; no alternate acceptance-function experiment.

assumptions.name: Framework simulators
assumptions.description: Users can access S1 to generate ω1 from Pθ and S2 to generate ω2 conditionally on θ, θ-prime, ω1.

assumptions.name: Proposal density
assumptions.description: Each Qω1(θ,·) is assumed to have density qω1 with respect to λ.

assumptions.name: PoissonMH bounded contributions
assumptions.description: Algorithm 5 requires each φi(θ;x) in [0, Mi].

assumptions.name: TunaMH local bound
assumptions.description: Algorithm 6 requires a symmetric M and ci bound on each Ui difference.

evidence.anchor: for some symmetric non-negative function M

assumptions.name: Independent-data scope
assumptions.description: The tall-data target and current algorithms are framed for independent-data likelihoods.

experimental_design.name: Research-question sequence
experimental_design.description: Three experiments test tall-data Poisson variants in two synthetic settings and Tuna–SGLD in Bayesian MNIST logistic regression; a fourth subsection checks empirical correctness.

experimental_design.name: Heterogeneous truncated Gaussian
experimental_design.description: d=20, N=10^5, diagonal covariance, θ=(0,...,0), truncation [-3,3]^d, flat prior, β=10^-5; seven methods including SGLD.

experimental_design.name: Gaussian controls and metrics
experimental_design.description: Minibatch λ=0.0005L^2 gives about 6000 points; SGLD minibatch is 512; initial θ0 is N(0,Id); acceptance targets are 0.25, 0.4, 0.55 after pilot tuning; MSE and autocorrelation ESS are reported per dimension.

experimental_design.name: Robust linear regression
experimental_design.description: Student-t likelihood with d=10, N=10^5, v=4, β=10^-4, R=15; compares Poisson variants, full-batch methods, HMC and SGLD.

experimental_design.name: Bayesian logistic regression
experimental_design.description: MNIST 3s/5s uses 11,552 training and 1,902 test examples and first 50 PCs; Tuna–SGLD gradient batch size is 20, χ=10^-5, and the stated four step sizes are varied.

experimental_design.name: Correctness check
experimental_design.description: Reference posterior samples are generated by rejection sampling; matched computation budget, 20% burn-in, and two-sample KS comparisons are used.

experimental_design.name: Replication granularity
experimental_design.description: Code URL is in the abstract; Appendix C–F provides thinning, proposal, bound, and model derivations.

evidence.anchor: code to reproduce the experimental results

experimental_design.name: Seeds, hardware, versions
experimental_design.description: The PDF gives neither random seeds nor hardware/software versions; this is an absence claim over the analyzed document.

evidence.anchor: code to reproduce the experimental results

experimental_design.name: Data leakage control
experimental_design.description: The paper does not state a separate leakage-control protocol. The synthetic design and train/test counts are described, but no such protocol is named.

result_inventory.claim: On the heterogeneous truncated Gaussian, Poisson–Barker and Poisson–MALA are the top two methods in Table 1 best ESS/s.
result_inventory.comparison: Best min/median/max ESS/s over target acceptance rates 0.25, 0.4, 0.55.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Autocorrelation-based ESS by dimension, then min/median/max; Table 1 reports best-over-rate values and 100-run averages.
result_inventory.author_interpretation: Gradient-based minibatch proposals offer substantial benefits from more efficient proposals.
result_inventory.adverse_explanation: Poisson–MALA is worse than PoissonMH at target rate 0.25.

result_inventory.claim: On robust linear regression, Poisson–MALA has the largest reported best ESS/s.
result_inventory.comparison: Seven/eight-method comparison including full-batch MH/MALA/Barker/HMC, PoissonMH variants, and SGLD.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Table 2 min/median/max ESS/s and Figure 1 MSE over time, with 100-run averages.
result_inventory.author_interpretation: Poisson–MALA and Poisson–Barker improve 1.80–8.79 times over PoissonMH and approach/exceed 100 times full-batch performance.
result_inventory.adverse_explanation: The evidence is a synthetic model under pilot-tuned steps and the main table omits uncertainty intervals.

result_inventory.claim: Tuna–SGLD converges faster in clock time than TunaMH at all tested MNIST 3s/5s step sizes.
result_inventory.value: Qualitative curve claim; no scalar summary is printed in the main text.
result_inventory.comparison: Tuna–SGLD versus TunaMH and full-batch methods; HMC is reported to mix poorly for the tested steps.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Test-accuracy-over-time curves; Appendix G.4 adds time and iteration comparisons under wider/optimal tuning.
result_inventory.author_interpretation: Extra gradient minibatch yields faster convergence.
result_inventory.adverse_explanation: Appendix Figure 11 states MALA has superior iteration-wise convergence, separating per-iteration mixing from clock-time efficiency.

result_inventory.claim: The correctness check distinguishes the exact methods from fixed-step SGLD on the truncated Gaussian benchmark.
result_inventory.value: Poisson–Barker and Poisson–MALA maximum KS at most 0.05; SGLD maximum KS 0.18.
result_inventory.comparison: PoissonMH, Poisson–Barker, Poisson–MALA, full-batch MH/MALA/Barker, and SGLD against rejection-sampling reference samples.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Two-sample KS after matched computation budget and 20% burn-in, summarized by dimension min/median/max.
result_inventory.author_interpretation: Supports sampling from the correct target in this benchmark.
result_inventory.adverse_explanation: A single finite benchmark check cannot establish finite-run correctness for every model.

evidence.anchor: maximum KS statistics no larger than 0.05

result_inventory.claim: Additional large-N and 50-dimensional experiments retain the claimed ranking trend.
result_inventory.value: For 50-D Table 7, Poisson–MALA best ESS/s is (13.92, 14.91, 15.58); Poisson–Barker is (6.07, 6.51, 6.84).
result_inventory.comparison: Same robust-regression method set at higher dimensionality and larger N.
result_inventory.statistical_method: Figures 6–9 and Tables 6–7; captions report 10-run averages for the 50-D results.
result_inventory.author_interpretation: All conclusions remain valid at higher dimensionality.
result_inventory.adverse_explanation: These are still related bounded/i.i.d. synthetic settings.

claim_closure.claim: Exchange, PoissonMH, and TunaMH can be unified under a common auxiliary-variable procedure.
claim_closure.method_response: Section 2 defines the procedure and Equation (1); Section 3 incorporates it as Case 1.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Appendix B.2 verifies all three examples algebraically.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Section 6 does not repeat the claim, but no missing method/theory response remains.

evidence.anchor: unified into a simple common procedure

claim_closure.claim: Two auxiliary variables can enable gradient-informed minibatch proposals while preserving the target distribution.
claim_closure.method_response: Algorithm 1 and Cases 2–3; Algorithms 2–3 instantiate the construction.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Proposition 2 supplies conditional reversibility; Table 3 offers one benchmark correctness check.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Section 6 states bound, tuning, and i.i.d. limitations.

claim_closure.claim: The new gradient-based minibatch algorithms outperform existing methods.
claim_closure.method_response: Algorithms 2 and 3 specify the two proposed families.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Tables 1–2, Figure 2, and Appendix G cover three task families and tuning variants.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: Section 6 says the source of empirical speedups remains unclear.

evidence.anchor: source of empirical speedups remains unclear

claim_closure.claim: The framework simplifies and extends theory for existing algorithms.
claim_closure.method_response: Theorem 1/2 and Propositions 3–5 specialize the framework.
claim_closure.evidence_response: The claim is formal and is not directly testable by the paper’s numerical design.

claim_closure.claim: Metropolized Tuna–SGLD addresses fixed-step SGLD bias using only minibatch data.
claim_closure.method_response: Algorithm 3 applies the independent gradient and ratio minibatches within Algorithm 1.
claim_closure.evidence_response: Proposition 2 supplies the conditional exactness proof; Table 3 separates KS behavior in one benchmark.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: No all-model finite-run claim is made.

claim_closure.claim: The approach should extend to non-i.i.d. models or weak/unavailable bounds.
claim_closure.method_response: No construction for these settings is given.
claim_closure.evidence_response: No theorem or experiment tests these settings.
claim_closure.conclusion_response: They are explicitly named future directions.

final_judgment.single_storyline: The paper rewrites costly target or gradient evaluation as an auxiliary-variable simulation-and-cancellation problem, then assigns one auxiliary variable to proposal guidance and another to ratio correction.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: The common procedure, Algorithms 1–3, the transition-density comparison, the central task settings/results, and a direct Section 6 limitation list remain in the nine-page main body.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Proofs, instance verification, Poisson thinning, proposal derivations, model-bound derivations, full rate-by-rate tables, and most sensitivity/robustness figures move to pages 12–35.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Each conceptual extension has a visible operational object: common procedure with Proposition 1, two-variable framework with Proposition 2, comparison theory with Theorem 1/2, then matching task-family evidence.
final_judgment.largest_gap: Formal proof and full tuning heterogeneity require appendix reading; the main best-over-rate tables compress sensitivity, and there is no direct empirical spectral-gap test.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For a unifying algorithmic framework, map each added degree of freedom to a concrete computational role, a condition preserving the target distribution, and an experiment that isolates the expected performance consequence.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: Use this rule when simulator access, estimator conditions, and cost assumptions can be checked. This paper relies on tight bounds, independent-data likelihoods, tuning choices, and controlled benchmarks.
